title: The Spectre of Moral Disengagement: What It Is, Why It Matters
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart explains moral disengagement — Albert Bandura's term for the rationalizations people use to vilify opponents while preserving their own self-image as good — using a Kalmoe and Mason survey finding that 40-60% of Americans express morally disengaged views toward the opposing political party. He illustrates the pattern in both student and teacher self-talk ("Teachers are terrible," "Administrators are only in it for the money") and argues moral disengagement is corrosive both externally, fueling cruelty and oppression, and internally, atrophying the disengager's own capacity to reason and love. Drawing on Gandhi and King, he argues that effective resistance to real, documented oppression was built not on moral disengagement but on moral engagement — the deliberate humanization of one's opponents — and that this, not hatred, proved the more powerful and durable engine for change. He closes by tying moral disengagement to his broader philosophy that education should promote flourishing, arguing that ignoring the moral dimension of human life is a real cost to both students and teachers.
points: Stuart grounds the concept in Bandura's 1996 research and a Kalmoe/Mason survey finding 40-60% of Americans express moral disengagement toward the opposing political party — a scale he calls troubling.

He gives concrete, classroom-relevant examples of moral disengagement in both student self-talk ("This whole school system is garbage") and teacher self-talk ("Administrators are only in it for the money").

His central historical argument: Gandhi and King's resistance movements were built on moral engagement — the deliberate humanization of oppressors — rather than the moral disengagement that might seem more intuitive under real oppression.
He frames moral disengagement as harmful to the disengager as well as the target, comparing its long-term effect on empathy and reasoning to smoking or refusing to exercise.
quotes: In a recent paper presented at the NCAPSA American Politics Meeting, researchers Nathan Kalmoe and Lilliana Mason shared findings from a nationally representative survey: 40-60% of Americans express moral disengagement with members of the political party opposed to their own.

In other words, when we catch ourselves habitually emphasizing our innocence/goodness and emphasizing the guilt/badness of the people or groups against us, we're morally disengaging. We magnify our goodness and our enemy's faults.
But the harm of moral disengagement is internal, too — it harms the disengager. When we morally disengage, we atrophy our ability to reason, to empathize, to love.
Gandhi's writings speak to moral engagement — the humanization of his enemies. "In the dictionary of satyagraha, there is no enemy…" Gandhi writes.

King had this same penchant for the humanization of his oppressors. In Chapter 5 of Strength to Love, he argues that "we must recognize that the evil deeds of the enemy-neighbor, the thing that hurts, never quite expresses all that he is.
Gandhi and King agreed: moral disengagement must have no quarter with us if we aim to produce a more just society.

Moral disengagement is a cancer in the flourishing life. If we have a philosophy here on the blog — a systematic way of thinking about our work — then it's that the purpose of education is to promote the long-term flourishing of young people by teaching them toward a mastery of the disciplines.
